title: Professional Scepticism
author: David Didau
summary: Didau argues that teaching is peculiarly vulnerable to bad ideas not because teachers are credulous but because human reasoning is systematically biased and experience alone cannot reliably detect whether a practice works. Professional scepticism is the disciplined habit of questioning claims: what evidence supports them, how was the evidence generated, what would count against the claim? Science can help test claims about learning once aims are agreed, but it cannot settle by itself what schooling is for. Questions about purpose (transmission, employability, civic formation, flourishing) are moral and political. Didau's practical closing is a checklist for leaders: can we define the problem, what evidence suggests the intervention will work, how will we know if it works, when should we expect improvement, what if goals are not met, what will teachers do less of, are we respecting teacher expertise? The list is modest but serious, protecting time and trust while reframing scepticism as an ethical obligation.
points: Professional scepticism is not hostility to evidence; it is the disciplined habit of questioning claims: what evidence supports this, how was it generated, what would count against it?
Human reasoning is systematically biased; confirmation bias guarantees that experience alone will never separate what works from what only feels as if it does.
Scepticism should guard against premature rejection as well as premature adoption; a healthy profession welcomes challenge rather than treating it as disloyalty.
quotes: Until education becomes the kind of profession that reveres evidence, we should not be surprised to find its experts dispensing unproven methods, endlessly flitting from one fad to another. The greatest victims of these fads are the very students who are most at risk.
Science can help us understand what is. It is far less helpful when it comes to deciding what ought to be. Facts about the world do not contain values hidden inside them, waiting to be discovered.

To be professional sceptical is to engage in the disciplined habit of questioning claims by asking what evidence supports them, how that evidence was generated, and what would count against the claim being true.

We are not neutral judges of our own ideas. We are inclined to defend beliefs we have invested time, effort or reputation in. We discount evidence that challenges us and overvalue evidence that confirms what we already think.

The aim of research should not be to prove ourselves right but to find out where we are wrong. Randomised controlled trials, laboratory experiments and meta analyses matter because they are designed to falsify claims, not to endorse them.
Scepticism must cut both ways: it should guard us against premature rejection as well as premature adoption.
Every untested claim adopted in good faith carries an opportunity cost. Time spent on ineffective practice is time not spent on something better.

If teaching is to rise above the level of homeopathy, professional scepticism has to be seen as an ethical obligation rather than an optional extra. Children deserve more than confidence and conviction.” Archived from David Didau on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
